_meta.description: Estimated (tag E) coefficients for the Squib physics model. None of these is Squib-specific measured data. They are prototype values chosen from general naval-architecture practice and are meant to be recalibrated when performance evidence arrives (docs/MISSING_INFORMATION.md B2-B5). See docs/PHYSICS.md for how each is used.

crewMassEach.note: Per person; crew count from class-spec

yawRadiusOfGyrationFrac.note: k_zz / LOA, typical small keelboat range 0.24-0.30

addedMassSwayFrac.note: Fin keel + canoe body, slender-body order of magnitude

aboveMinimum.note: Boat weight above the class minimum (minBoatMass). 0 for the Rondar default; data/boats/squib/variants.json sets it for other builds

mastX.note: Mast position forward of the centre of gravity

mainCEHeight.note: Mainsail centre of effort above waterline

mainCEChordFrac.note: CE position along the boom from the mast

jibFoot.note: Derived from area 6.0 m2 and an assumed luff of about 5.7 m

lateralX.note: Effective centre of the combined keel + canoe-body lift, forward of the CG. The canoe body produces its side force well forward, so the hydrodynamic centre lies ahead of the geometric centre of lateral resistance. Chosen so the boat carries slight weather helm that grows with wind (about 1 deg at 10 kn and 3 deg at 15 kn close-hauled) and rounds up slowly with the helm centred, which is the usual design intent; not measured.

rudderX.note: Transom-hung rudder assumed; arrangement not established

crewLateralOut.note: Sitting out on the windward side deck

clMax.note: Typical published peak lift coefficients for mainsails are of order 1.3-1.6

stallWidthDeg.note: Blend width from attached to flat-plate behaviour

effectiveAR.note: Includes deck end-plate effect, reduced for twist

alphaLuffStartDeg.note: Below this chord incidence the sail is fully luffing. Soft cambered sails luff at a larger chord angle than a flat foil because the luff entry angle is several degrees above the chord line

alphaFullDeg.note: Above this chord incidence the sail is fully drawing

sheetMinDeg.note: Boom angle with the sheet hard in

autoTrimAlphaDeg.note: Target incidence used by the auto-trim assist

jibBlanketStartAwaDeg.note: Jib starts to be blanketed by the main when running

byTheLeeMainDeg.note: How far by the lee the apparent wind must be before the twisted mainsail inverts and the boom is driven across (gybe onset). A rigid-sail model cannot produce this leech flip itself; the swing across is then dynamic.

byTheLeeJibDeg.note: Jib changes side this far by the lee (kinematic jib)

boomGain.note: Jib only: first-order response of the jib to its target angle (the main boom is a dynamic body)

jibDownwashOnMainDeg.note: Jib downwash reduces the main's incidence (main backwinds when pinching). Qualitative effect documented in sail-interaction literature (e.g. Gentry 1971); magnitude estimated. Fades out by a beam reach.

mainUpwashOnJibDeg.note: Main upwash increases the jib's incidence; magnitude estimated

boomInertia.note: Boom, mainsail and fittings about the mast axis

boomMassMoment.note: Mass x distance of the boom and sail centre of mass from the mast (gravity swings the boom to leeward when heeled)

boomDamping.note: Mechanical damping at the gooseneck and sheet blocks (aerodynamic damping emerges from the sail forces)

boomRestitution.note: Bounce when the boom fetches up against the sheet or shrouds

residuaryTable.note: Parametric curve shaped like moderate-displacement hull data (L/vol^(1/3) about 5.5). Placeholder for a Delft-series (DSYHS) regression once hull parameters and coefficient tables are sourced.

lateralArea.note: Keel plus equivalent hull lifting area

lateralAR.note: Effective aspect ratio including hull mirror effect

rudderArea.note: About 0.75 m span x 0.30 m chord

rudderRateDegS.note: How fast the helm can move the tiller

hullDraft.note: Canoe body draft for cross-flow drag strips

rudderFlowStraightening.note: Fraction of the hull's leeway removed from the rudder inflow by the keel's downwash (0 = none, 1 = rudder sees no leeway). Typical manoeuvring-model values are of order 0.3-0.6.

rudderVentStartDeg.note: Heel beyond which the rudder starts to lose grip: heeled, it works nearer the surface and draws air down its low-pressure side (ventilation) or lifts partly out. Practitioner accounts describe sudden loss of steering at large heel, after which the boat rounds up and comes upright (PBO 'Broaching' and others: SOURCES.md R3). No Squib measurement.

rudderVentEndDeg.note: Heel by which the rudder has lost most of its grip (it keeps rudderVentResidual of it)

rudderVentResidual.note: Share of the rudder's force left when fully ventilated

gm.note: Metacentric height: initial slope of the GZ curve (righting arm = GM sin(phi) at small angles)

gzTable.note: Righting arm GZ versus heel. Initial slope matches GM; shape typical of a ballasted fin-keel dayboat (maximum near 50-60 deg, vanishing stability near 117 deg). Not from a Squib stability test.

rollRadiusOfGyration.note: k_xx including mast and rig high up and the keel low down

rollLinearDamping.note: Hull and appendage roll damping not already produced by the keel and sail forces (those emerge from the roll motion itself); about 5% of critical

rudderDepth.note: Centre of rudder force below the waterline (roll arm)

bowContactX.note: Forward contact point (stem), body x from the CG

bowContactDepth.note: Depth of the forefoot below the waterline

sternContactDepth.note: Depth of the rudder's lowest point below the waterline (transom-hung rudder; not established)

keelContactX.note: Keel tip position along the hull; its depth is the class draft (S)

waterplaneArea.note: LWL x beam x 0.5: sets how fast weight transfers to the ground as the water falls (rho g A per metre)

friction.note: Coulomb friction between keel/hull and mud or sand

damping.note: Viscous term at a contact point (keel ploughing into mud), reaching full value at 0.05 m penetration. Chosen so a boat that touches the bottom stops within a few seconds rather than bumping along the bank

slopeLimit.note: Cap on the bed slope used for the down-slope push (8 m grid turns quay walls into ramps)

selfDraining.note: Rondar cockpit (default): 1 = self-draining (water runs out through the transom outlets); 0 = water stays until bailed (Hunter and Parker builds)

deckEdgeY.note: Half-breadth of the rail (side-deck outer edge) at the cockpit: half the class beam

deckEdgeZ.note: Height of the rail above the waterline at the cockpit (no lines plan; same estimate as the 3D model)

cockpitEdgeY.note: Half-width of the cockpit opening (inner edge of the side deck)

cockpitEdgeZ.note: Height of the cockpit edge above the waterline (deck camber; estimate)

railSlop.note: With the rail under but the cockpit edge still clear, this fraction of the water running onto the side deck slops on into the cockpit

toeRail.note: Water must rise this far over the rail (toe rail) before it runs onto the side deck

inflowLength.note: Length of the cockpit side (and of side deck) over which water runs in

weirCoefficient.note: Broad-crested weir, Q = C L h^1.5 (C = 2/3 Cd sqrt(2g), Cd 0.61)

sprayRate.note: Spray and slop shipped when sailing into waves: rate per metre of significant wave height above sprayStartHs, at 2 m/s through the water, head-on

sprayStartHs.note: Significant wave height below which no water comes aboard

soleWidth.note: Width of the cockpit floor where shipped water collects

soleAboveCG.note: Height of the cockpit floor above the centre of gravity. Rondar: a raised self-draining floor above the waterline; the CG is low (375 kg iron keel, about 0.25 m below the waterline, E)

drainArea.note: Self-draining cockpit: total outlet area through the transom (orifice, Cd 0.61); used only when selfDraining = 1. Sized so a cockpit sheds water slopping in over a buried rail (estimate)

bailRate.note: Crew bailing by hand (about a litre every two seconds) once the water passes bailStart

bailStart.note: Water in the boat before the crew starts bailing

capacity.note: Cockpit full (swamped): buoyancy keeps the boat afloat, no more water comes in
